response.consequence: When the device limit is reached, a legitimate already-registered anonymous device that sends a repeat request with unchanged values can be rejected with a limit error. Authenticate then fails for a user who should be allowed. The window is narrow, so the impact is limited.
response.explanation: updateDevice maps every result with rowsAffected == 0 to ErrDeviceLimitReached. A zero count does not mean the device is missing. go-sql-driver/mysql returns changed rows rather than matched rows unless clientFoundRows is set. An existing device in the window whose client_ip, user_agent and updated_at all equal the stored values therefore reports 0. That happens when a second request from the same device arrives in the same timestamp second (the column is second precision), or when the caller passes an identical UpdatedAt. The code cannot tell this case from a device that is absent or expired. I did not read the caller to check how it sets UpdatedAt. I also did not check the driver DSN configuration for clientFoundRows.
response.title: Zero affected rows is reported as device limit reached even for existing devices

response.consequence: With the anonymous device limit reached, an over-limit device gets one failed request and then full anonymous access, so the limit is not enforced. Behaviour is also inconsistent: the same device alternates between rejected and allowed depending on cache state.
response.explanation: Authenticate now returns ErrDeviceLimitReached to reject anonymous requests at the limit. TagDevice reaches tagDeviceUI in anonimpl/impl.go. That function calls localCache.SetDefault(key) at line 87, before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (database.go:96), the cache entry has already been written. The next request from the same device hits the cache at line 83 and TagDevice returns nil. Authenticate then returns an anonymous identity, so the over-limit device is let in. The error is not wrapped, so errors.Is does match on the first call. The failure is that enforcement is not stable. A new device is rejected once, then admitted until the cache entry expires. Rejection also depends on whether the cache entry exists, not on the limit.
response.title: Device-limit rejection is only returned once per device; the local cache then lets repeat requests through

response.consequence: Under concurrent traffic from new anonymous devices, the configured device limit can be exceeded. The limit is an enforcement control, so this lets it be bypassed.
response.explanation: CreateOrUpdateDevice calls CountDevices and then runs a separate INSERT, or the Postgres/MySQL upsert, with no transaction, lock or conditional insert between the two. Suppose the count is limit-1 and N requests from distinct new device IDs arrive at once. Each reads count < limit, skips updateDevice, and inserts its own row. The Postgres and MySQL upserts only key on device_id, so they do not enforce the limit either. The table can end up with limit-1+N active devices.
response.title: Device limit check is not atomic with the insert/upsert

The value is non-sensitive configuration, and exposing it is not a concrete defect.

The same device's next request hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil, and Authenticate returns an anonymous identity. The device gets anonymous access without being stored, so it is never counted.
